cards.title: The book that doesn't exist
cards.body:
You ask a chatbot for a book about volcanoes. It suggests "Fire Below" by Dr Helen Marsh, with a short summary. It sounds perfect.

You search the library. There's no such book, and no such author. The chatbot made it up, and sounded completely sure.

cards.title: Fluent, confident, wrong
cards.body:
When a chatbot writes something false but says it smoothly and confidently, it's called a **hallucination**.

It happens because the model picks tokens that **sound** likely, not tokens it has checked are true. A book title, an author's name and a summary are all very likely-sounding things to write. If the true answer isn't in its patterns, it still writes something that looks like an answer.

Hallucinations are most common with specific details: names, dates, numbers, quotes and sources. They're also more likely when a model has mostly read one kind of text. Imagine a small model trained on space adventure stories, full of sentences like "Captain Rivera stepped onto Mars".

cards.prompt: That small space-story model gets this text. Which word is it **most likely** to write next?
cards.context: The first person to walk on Mars was
cards.hint: It isn't choosing what's true. What did this model read again and again?
cards.nudge: Think about the stories this model learned from. Which word filled this spot in them?
cards.explanation: Nobody has walked on Mars yet, and Neil Armstrong walked on the **Moon**. But in this model's space stories, sentences like this carry on with "**Captain** …", so it's likely to invent a Mars walker: a hallucination, built one likely token at a time. (Bigger chatbots have seen this question and usually get it right; the risk is highest for things they've seen less.)

cards.title: How to check
cards.body:
For anything that matters, check it yourself:

- **Find it in a trusted source**: a textbook, a library catalogue, an official website.
- **Ask for sources, then open them**: chatbots can invent sources too, so make sure each one really exists and says what the chatbot claims.
- **Be extra careful with details**: names, dates, numbers and quotes.
- **Health questions**: ask a doctor, a pharmacist or a trusted adult.

Asking the chatbot "are you sure?", or asking again, doesn't check anything: it can repeat the same mistake, or change a right answer.

cards.prompt: You're writing a report on volcanoes.

steps.text: A chatbot suggests the book "Fire Below" by Dr Helen Marsh, and gives you a quote from it for your report. What do you do?

choices.text: Use the quote: it's from a book
choices.consequence: Your teacher can't find the book anywhere, because it doesn't exist. A made-up quote in a report is a real problem.

choices.text: Search for the book in the library catalogue
choices.consequence: No results, for the book or the author.

choices.text: Ask the chatbot if the book is real
choices.consequence: It says "Yes, it's a well-known book!" It can be just as confident about a hallucination.

steps.text: The library has never heard of it. What now?

choices.text: Leave it out, and find a real source in the library
choices.consequence: Right: the book was a hallucination. A real source gives you facts you can trust, and quote.

choices.text: Keep the quote, but don't say where it's from
choices.consequence: The quote is made up too, so it's still not true, and now it's hidden. Use a real source.

cards.hint: Look back at how to check. What's a trusted source for whether a book exists?
cards.explanation: Book titles, authors and quotes are classic hallucinations. **Check them in a trusted source**, like a library catalogue. Asking the chatbot doesn't help: it can be confidently wrong about its own mistakes.

cards.title: A short memory
cards.body:
A chatbot can only look at a limited amount of text at once: your messages and its replies so far. This is called its **context window**.

In a very long chat, the earliest messages can fall out of the window, or get less attention, so it can "forget" something you said at the start, like "keep answers short". A brand-new chat usually starts with an empty window, unless the app has a memory feature.

cards.prompt: Would you **double-check** each thing a chatbot gives you, or is it **fine to use** as it is?

items.label: A date for your history project
A quote from a famous scientist
A website it says it got facts from

cards.hint: Ask: if it were made up, would it matter? Details like names, dates, quotes and sources are where hallucinations hide.
cards.nudge: Ideas can't really be wrong. Facts, quotes, sources and anything about health can be, and it matters.
cards.explanation: Dates, quotes, sources and anything about health are **facts** that could be hallucinated, and getting them wrong matters, so double-check. Medicine questions go to a doctor, a pharmacist or a trusted adult. Ideas for themes, rhymes and titles are fine: there's no "wrong" to catch.

cards.prompt: A chatbot tells you a fact you need for an assignment. What's the **best** way to check it?

options.text: Find it in a trusted source, like a textbook or an official website
Ask the same question again and see if the two answers match
options.nudge: A chatbot can repeat the same mistake. Where can you check it outside the chatbot?

options.text: Ask the chatbot to explain how it knows, and if it's sure
options.nudge: It can be confidently wrong about its own mistakes. Where else could you look?

options.text: Ask a different chatbot and see if it gives the same answer
options.nudge: Another chatbot can make the same kind of mistake. Where can you check outside chatbots?

cards.hint: Look back at how to check: the answer has to come from outside the chatbot.
cards.explanation: Only a **trusted source** outside chatbots really checks a fact. Asking again, asking it how it knows, or asking a different chatbot all stay inside chatbots, which can repeat or defend a hallucination.

cards.prompt: A chatbot tells you a famous ship sank in **1915**, and gives a link to a museum website.

steps.text: You click the link, and it opens a real museum page about the ship. What now?

choices.text: Use 1915: the link works, so it's checked
choices.consequence: The page is real, but you didn't read it. It actually says the ship sank in **1912**. A real link isn't proof of the claim.

choices.text: Read the page and find the date it gives
Ask the chatbot to double-check its date
choices.consequence: It apologises and says 1914. Still not checked: the answer is on the page you already have.

steps.text: The museum page says 1912. The chatbot said 1915. Which do you use?

choices.consequence: Right: the trusted source you actually read wins.

choices.text: 1915: the chatbot found the page, so it knows
choices.consequence: The chatbot linked the right page but wrote the wrong date. Go with what the source really says.

cards.hint: Look back at how to check: a source has to really exist **and** say what the chatbot claims.
cards.explanation: A link that works isn't enough: chatbots can link a real page and still get the detail wrong. **Read the source**, and go with what it actually says.

cards.prompt: You're using a chatbot to practise for a quiz.

steps.text: At the start you said: "Don't tell me the answers, just give hints." Two hours and hundreds of messages later, it starts giving you the answers. Why, and what do you do?

choices.text: It's ignoring you on purpose, so give up
choices.consequence: It isn't doing it on purpose. In a long chat, your first message may have fallen out of its context window.

choices.text: It may have lost track of your instruction, so repeat it
choices.consequence: Exactly. In a long chat, early messages can fall out of its context window or get less attention. Reminding it, or starting a fresh chat with the instruction first, fixes it.

choices.text: It's broken, so it's lying now
choices.consequence: It isn't broken or lying. It can only look at a limited amount of the chat at once.

cards.hint: What happens to the earliest messages in a very long chat?
cards.explanation: In a long chat, early messages can fall out of the context window or get less attention, so it can lose track of your instruction. **Repeat it**, or start a new chat with it first.

cards.prompt: Match each problem to what to do about it.

pairs.left: Says where a fact came from
pairs.right: Open the source and read it

cards.hint: Each fix uses something outside the chatbot, except one. Which problem is about the chatbot's memory?
cards.nudge: Think about each one: is it a fact to check, a source to open, a memory problem, or something only an expert should answer?
cards.explanation: Books get checked in a **catalogue**; sources get **opened and read**; medicine questions go to a **doctor or pharmacist**; and a forgotten instruction gets **repeated**, because it fell out of the context window.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **hallucination** is a fluent, confident answer that's false, because the model picks likely tokens, not checked facts.
- They hide in details: names, dates, numbers, quotes, sources.
- Check things that matter in a trusted source; asking the chatbot again doesn't check anything.
- The **context window** is how much of the chat it can see at once; in long chats it can forget the start.

Next: the module quiz.
